metadata.title: Reading the Screen
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: How a shader reads what is already drawn
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: lecture skill: opens on the narrated identity card then the hesitant writer; no composer cold open.
metadata.source_doc: Godot 4.7 documentation (Screen-reading shaders, CanvasItem shaders, CanvasLayer, BackBufferCopy, Control); Godot 4.7.2 on Apple M4 Pro (evidence/planning-checks); see SOURCES.md

beats.narration_text: Reading the Screen. Learn how a shader can read what the game has already drawn, so you can filter the whole screen, bend the picture, and build water you can see through.

routing.reason: The lecture skill's approved first beat: portrait, title, narrated summary.

shot.visual_intent: Professor Bear portrait, exact film title and short payoff visible immediately.

show.event: Complete populated lecture opener visible for the whole narration

qc.sparse_reason: Identity card: portrait and title; teaching motion resumes in BIDEA.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Most people think a shader only knows its own sprite. One line of code breaks that rule. A shader can read what is already on screen, and build on it.

show.event: backspaces 'its own sprite' and types 'what is already on screen'

props.text:
A shader only knows
its own sprite.

beats.motion_claim: The writer types the assumption a newcomer arrives with and corrects it into the film's real subject.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. A texture is an image a shader can read. U V is a point's address on a shape: zero to one across, zero to one down. A uniform is a value your game sets from outside. Fragment is the function that runs once for each pixel and sets its color. Draw order is what gets drawn first; later things cover earlier ones. And post-processing is changing the picture after it is drawn.

terms.meaning: an image a shader can read by address
a point's address on the shape: 0 to 1 across, 0 to 1 down
a value your game sets from outside; every pixel sees the same one
runs once for each pixel the shape covers; sets its color
what is drawn first; later things cover earlier ones
changing the picture after it is drawn

qc.sparse_reason: TERMS card: prerequisites, one plain line each.

beats.act: I · A Copy of the Screen
beats.narration_text: Give a sprite a shader, and it can color that sprite. But glass, heat haze and water do something different. They change what is behind them. For that, a shader has to read the picture the game has already drawn.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'A Copy of the Screen' (serif 40) top-left. A real Godot render in a framed window on the cream stage: a meadow of green checker tiles, a sand path, flowers, and in the lower left a pool whose wavy top edge ripples and whose water bends the checker lines and the path behind it. The teal player stands to the right. A terracotta ring settles on the pool.

show.event: meadow with the live pool; act title top-left
terracotta ring settles on the pool

beats.act: I · A Copy of the Screen
beats.narration_text: There is a catch. Graphics hardware cannot properly read a picture while it is drawing into it. So Godot copies the picture drawn so far, and your shader reads the copy. That copy is the screen texture.

shot.visual_intent: On the cream stage a 16:9 screen frame, left, fills in the order the game draws it: the green checker ground, a tree, a flower, then a small rectangle labelled 'shader'. Just before that rectangle is drawn, a camera-flash snapshot copies the whole frame into a second frame on the right, labelled 'screen texture: a copy of everything drawn so far'. A drawn arrow runs from the shader rectangle to the copy.

show.event: screen frame; ground, tree, flower drawn in order
flash: the frame is copied to the right
arrow from the shader rectangle to the copy

shot.motion_claim: The frame is copied in one flash and the shader's arrow reads from the copy, not from the live frame.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: A snapshot being taken is a motion, and the arrow into the copy is the claim; an isometric flow would show boxes, not a copy of a picture.

beats.act: I · A Copy of the Screen
beats.narration_text: Here is the smallest use. In the fragment function, each pixel's color becomes whatever the screen holds at that pixel's spot. Switch it on, and the rectangle vanishes. It is still there. It only shows what is behind it.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left with the 7-line shader; at right a real Godot window on the meadow: a plain teal rectangle in a cream frame. At 58 percent the shader switches on and the teal fill vanishes, leaving the cream frame around meadow. Label: 'still there'.

show.event: the shader switches on; the teal fill vanishes

cues.label: fragment(): runs once for each pixel

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · shader switched on mid-clip (58 percent)

shot.motion_claim: The teal rectangle vanishes at the cue; the cream frame stays, empty, showing the meadow.

lecture.why: Code and its result side by side, with the vanishing as the proof; code alone cannot show that the rectangle is still there.
lecture.capture_spec: C02: scene_c02_window.gd, 1280 x 720 canvas through the 4K SubViewport route, 30 fps, Forward+, length = the beat's audio. A teal rectangle (0.38, 0.22, 0.30 x 0.30 of the canvas) in a cream frame; 01-window is assigned at u = 0.58. Verified: the rectangle's interior equals the meadow exactly (8,820 samples, worst channel difference 0).

beats.act: I · A Copy of the Screen
beats.narration_text: Now take the uniform line apart. A uniform is a value that comes from outside. Sampler two D is the type of a texture a shader can read. And the name is yours to choose.

shot.visual_intent: The line `uniform sampler2D screen_texture : hint_screen_texture;` set in monospace on the cream stage, each token its own object at explicit coordinates. A bracket is drawn under `uniform` with the label 'from outside'; one under `sampler2D` with 'sampler2D: the type of a texture a shader reads'; one under `screen_texture` with 'your name'. The `hint_screen_texture` token stays grey until the next beat.
shot.motion_claim: Each bracket is drawn under its token on the word that names it, so the line is read left to right.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: The pieces of one line need brackets under tokens; ShaderLab highlights whole lines only.

beats.act: I · A Copy of the Screen
beats.narration_text: Then the hint, after the colon. A hint is a word that tells Godot how to treat a uniform. This one says: fill it with the screen. Godot refreshes it every frame, so you never set it yourself.

shot.visual_intent: The same line again with the `hint_screen_texture` token ringed (terracotta ring, grey backing) and the labels 'hint: the word after a colon that tells Godot how to treat a uniform' and 'this one: fill it with the screen'. Below, a slot labelled `screen_texture`. On three frame ticks (a small counter 1, 2, 3) a fresh miniature of the meadow drops into the slot, replacing the last one; in each the flower has moved a little. A small cursor arrow outside the slot is crossed out: 'you never set it'.

show.event: first copy drops into the slot

shot.motion_claim: A new copy drops into the slot on every tick, replacing the old one, with nobody placing it.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: Replacement on every tick is the claim 'Godot refreshes it every frame'; a static diagram could not show that the copy changes.

beats.act: I · A Copy of the Screen
beats.narration_text: Now read it. The function texture takes a texture and an address, and returns the color stored there. Four numbers come back: red, green, blue, and alpha, which is how visible it is.

shot.visual_intent: The screen texture drawn as a 12 by 7 grid of outline cells in the meadow colours (cells are never filled behind text). A terracotta probe ring sits on one cell with a live label 'address (0.62, 0.40)'; a drawn arrow runs to a swatch showing that cell's colour. The probe hops to two more cells and the swatch follows. After the third hop the swatch splits into four chips R, G, B, A; the A chip carries 'alpha: how visible a pixel is (0 invisible, 1 solid)'.

show.event: swatch splits into R, G, B, A

shot.motion_claim: The probe hops from cell to cell and the swatch changes colour to match; then the swatch splits into four numbers.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: An address going in and a color coming out is a lookup, and a lookup is a probe on a grid; code would only name it.

beats.act: I · A Copy of the Screen
beats.narration_text: A pixel has two addresses. U V is its place on its own shape. Screen U V is its place on the whole screen. Slide the shape, and U V stays the same, while screen U V changes.

shot.visual_intent: A 16:9 screen outline with a smaller 4:3 shape inside it and one pixel dot on the shape. Two live labels follow the dot: 'UV (0.5, 0.5)', measured on the shape ('UV: a point's address on the shape'), and 'screen UV (0.31, 0.62)', measured on the screen ('SCREEN_UV: a pixel's address on the whole screen, not on its own shape'). The shape then slides right: the first label stays (0.5, 0.5) while the second counts up to (0.62, 0.62).

show.event: the shape slides; screen UV counts up

shot.motion_claim: The shape slides and one label never changes while the other counts up.

beats.act: I · A Copy of the Screen
beats.narration_text: Read the screen with U V, and the rectangle fills with a tiny copy of the whole screen. Read it with screen U V, and the rectangle becomes a window onto what is behind it, wherever it slides.

shot.visual_intent: Two 16:9 rectangles in cream frames, one above the other, slide right together over the meadow. The top one (UV) holds a tiny copy of the whole screen that does not move with the picture; the bottom one (screen UV) is a window onto the meadow. Right-margin labels 'UV' and 'screen UV'.

show.event: label 'screen UV' by the bottom rectangle

beats.act: I · A Copy of the Screen
beats.narration_text: Now change the color. Adding r g b after it keeps red, green and blue. One minus each of them flips every color. Slide the window, and the flipped picture stays pinned to the screen. Only the opening moves.

beats.act: I · A Copy of the Screen
beats.narration_text: Older tutorials use a shortcut called screen texture, in capital letters. Godot four removed it. The compiler says so, and points you to the hint instead. If an old line fails, this is why.

shot.visual_intent: A cream code card with the five-line shader that uses the capital-letters shortcut; focus lands on the line that uses it. Under the card the engine's own message, verbatim from a real run, is the note.

show.event: focus on the shader's first lines
settled: old line and the compiler's message

props.title: A line from older tutorials
props.note: Godot 4.7.2 compiler: SCREEN_TEXTURE has been removed in favor of using hint_screen_texture with a uniform.

shot.motion_claim: Focus steps down to the old line and stays on it while the compiler's message is read.

lecture.runner_up: BrowserCapture of the docs row 'SCREEN_TEXTURE: Removed in Godot 4'
lecture.why: The real message from a real run is the thing a viewer will actually see; the docs row says the same but is not what appears when it fails.

beats.narration_text: A full-screen effect, or post-processing, needs a node covering every pixel. A color rect with your shader on it can do that: set its layout to Full Rect. Its edges follow the screen's corners, even when the game is resized.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Full-Screen Effects' (serif 40) top-left. A screen outline (the game screen) with a small teal rectangle labelled 'ColorRect' inside it. Four terracotta anchor dots on the rectangle's corners fly out to the screen's four corners and the rectangle stretches to fill it; the label 'Layout > Anchors Preset: Full Rect' (the editor's own words) appears. The screen outline then grows wider and narrower in turn and the rectangle follows.

show.event: screen outline, small rectangle; act title
corner dots fly out; rectangle fills the screen

shot.motion_claim: Four dots fly to the four corners, the rectangle fills the screen, and it keeps filling it when the screen is resized.

lecture.why: Corners snapping to corners is a motion, and the follow-on resize is the point of anchors; the editor frame is an optional upgrade, recorded in CAPTURE-PLAN.

beats.narration_text: Put that color rect in a canvas layer. A canvas layer is a group drawn together, with a number. The game is at zero. A layer numbered one is drawn after it, so it can read everything the game drew.

shot.visual_intent: Two panes in an exploded side view: the lower pane 'game · 0' with a tiny meadow and player; the upper pane 'canvas layer 1' holding the full-rect colour rect, tinted pale grey, with the definition 'canvas layer: a group drawn together, with a number; higher is drawn later'. The lower pane slides in first, then the upper one is drawn on top of it with its number. A drawn arrow runs from the upper pane down through the lower: 'reads everything below'.

show.event: color rect inside a layer pane

shot.motion_claim: The panes arrive in order, zero then one, and the arrow shows the upper layer reading everything beneath it.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: Layers are a stack, and a stack with a drawing order is clearest as panes sliding into place.

beats.narration_text: One catch: a color rect catches mouse clicks, so your game never hears them. Set its mouse filter to Ignore, and the clicks pass through to the game.

shot.visual_intent: The two panes again, side view: the game pane below, the full-rect colour rect pane above, labelled 'Mouse > Filter: Stop' (the editor's own words). A click (a drawn arrow tip with an expanding ring) comes down from above and stops at the colour rect, which flashes. The label changes to 'Mouse > Filter: Ignore' and the next click passes through the colour rect to the game pane, which flashes.

show.event: label Ignore; click 2 reaches the game

shot.motion_claim: The first click stops at the rect; after the label changes the second click passes straight through.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: A click that stops or passes is a path, and a path is a drawn arrow; a Godot capture would need an input log nobody can see.

beats.narration_text: Start with gray. A gray pixel has equal red, green and blue. The function dot multiplies each by a weight and adds them up. Green weighs most and blue least, because that is how bright each color looks to us.

shot.visual_intent: One meadow pixel as a green swatch. Three horizontal bars show its red, green and blue values. Each bar is multiplied by a weight chip (0.299, 0.587, 0.114) and shrinks to a partial bar; the three partial bars then slide together end to end into one gray bar and a gray swatch appears beside the green one. The 0.587 chip is ringed last. Caption 'dot(a, b): multiply the matching parts and add them' (the GLOSSARY's wording).

show.event: bars join into one gray bar

shot.motion_claim: Three bars shrink by their weights and join end to end into one gray bar, and the gray swatch appears.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: A sum is three pieces becoming one, and that is a shape change, which Manim transforms rather than cuts.

beats.narration_text: Then mix. Mix blends two values by an amount: zero gives the first, one gives the second. Make the amount a uniform with a range hint, and your game can drain the color from the whole picture with one dial.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (the 10-line gray shader); at right a real Godot window: the meadow and the teal player under a full-screen filter. The amount uniform sweeps from 0 to 1 and the colour drains out of the whole picture, grass, path, flowers and player together.

cues.label: mix(a, b, t): blends from a to b: t of 0 gives a, 1 gives b

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · amount swept by script

shot.motion_claim: The colour drains from everything at once as the dial turns.

lecture.why: A dial turning is a continuous change and the whole picture draining is the claim; two stills would lose the dial.

beats.narration_text: Now a spotlight: color near the player, gray everywhere else. The shader needs two numbers from your game: where the player is, and how big the circle is. Both are uniforms.

beats.narration_text: Measure each pixel's distance from the player. The function distance gives the gap between two addresses. If it is more than the radius, make the pixel gray. Otherwise, leave it alone.

beats.narration_text: Look closely: it is an oval. Addresses run zero to one across and zero to one down, but the screen is wider than tall. So a step across is longer than a step down, and the circle stretches.

The square stretches sideways into a 16:9 screen rectangle and the circle becomes an ellipse. Two measurements appear along the ellipse: sideways '0.25 × 1280 = 320 px', up and down '0.25 × 720 = 180 px'. Caption 'oval'.

beats.narration_text: Screen pixel size is the size of one pixel, as a fraction of the screen. Its y divided by its x is the aspect ratio: width divided by height. Stretch both addresses across by that, and distances come out equal.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (the 14-line fixed spotlight); at right the same walk: the coloured area is an oval until 72 percent of the beat, when the shader is swapped and it becomes a circle.

aspect ratio: width divided by height

beats.narration_text: The shader cannot see your player. So every frame, your game takes the player's position on screen, divides it by the screen size, and sends it with set shader parameter. Move the player, and the circle follows.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left with the four-line GDScript _process; at right the finished circular spotlight following the walking player.

props.code:
func _process(_delta):
	var size := get_viewport_rect().size
	var on_screen: Vector2 = $Player.get_global_transform_with_canvas().origin
	$Layer/Filter.material.set_shader_parameter("player", on_screen / size)

cues.label: set_shader_parameter: sends a value to a uniform

beats.narration_text: So far, each pixel read the screen exactly where it sits. Read somewhere else, and the picture bends. Add a small number to the address, and every pixel shows what lies a little further right.

The shift uniform sweeps from 0 to 0.1 and the picture inside the frame slides sideways against the picture outside; the sand path breaks at the frame's edges. Label 'shift 0.1'.

beats.narration_text: Make the number depend on the row. Sine is a smooth wave between minus one and one. Feed it the vertical address, and each row gets a different push, left, then right. Straight lines now ripple.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (the 10-line ripple shader without time); at right a real Godot window: a large window in a cream frame; as the amount grows the straight tile edges inside become a chevron of ripples and the flowers stretch sideways.

cues.label: sin: a smooth wave between -1 and 1

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · amount grown by script

shot.motion_claim: Straight lines inside the frame start to ripple as the amount grows.

lecture.runner_up: manim plot of sin(y) with rows shifted
lecture.why: The real ripple is the claim; the plot would explain the function but not what a viewer will see in a game.
lecture.capture_spec: C10: scene_c10_ripple_still.gd, 1280 x 720 canvas through the 4K SubViewport route, 30 fps, Forward+, length = the beat's audio. Window 0.56 x 0.52 at (0.20, 0.08); amount 0 until u = 0.44, then 0.012 by u = 0.92. Verified: the tile edge in ten rows sits at 560 minus 0.01 sin(60 y) times 1280, within 0.5 px (0.6 in Compatibility; the edge is found to a whole pixel).

beats.narration_text: Add time inside the sine, and the ripples travel. Time is seconds on one clock shared by the whole game, so every pixel ripples in step.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (the 10-line ripple shader with TIME); at right the same large window with the ripples now travelling, live. Label 'time: one clock'.

cues.label: TIME: seconds on one clock shared by the whole game

beats.narration_text: A shader can only read what exists when the copy is taken. Godot takes it once, right before the first reading node on a layer is drawn. Everything drawn earlier is in it. Everything drawn later is not.

A camera flash fires just before 'reader 1' and a copy tile drops below the row, labelled 'the copy'. Tiles before the flash get a check mark; the tiles after it do not. An arrow from reader 2 points at the same copy tile, not a new one.

beats.narration_text: The fix is a node called Back Buffer Copy, placed between them, with its copy mode set to Viewport. It takes a fresh copy of the whole screen right there. Now the overlap flips back to the original colors.

beats.narration_text: The docs' examples add two more hints. Repeat disable means reading past the screen's edge gives the edge pixel, not the far side. Filter nearest asks for the exact pixel, no blending. The Forward Plus renderer obeys; Compatibility blends anyway.

The third label defines 'renderer' where the narration first says it; the capture is Forward+ (the video label says so), so the Compatibility half of the sentence is carried by the narration alone.

renderer: how Godot draws; your project picks one of three

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. The screen texture is a copy of what was drawn so far, read with screen U V. A color rect on a canvas layer covers every pixel, so one shader can filter the whole game. Read the screen at a shifted address, and the picture behind it bends. One copy is made for each layer, so draw order and layers decide what a shader can see.

show.event: recap lines land in narration order

A color rect on a canvas layer covers every pixel, so one shader can filter the whole game.
Read the screen at a shifted address, and the picture behind it bends.
One copy is made for each layer, so draw order and layers decide what a shader can see.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Write a Godot four canvas item shader for a full-screen color rect that turns everything behind it gray. One float uniform called amount, from zero to one: at zero nothing changes, at one it is fully gray. Read the screen with a screen texture hint, never the old built-in. Then point to the line that reads the screen. Now check two things yourself. Does the line that reads the screen use a screen texture hint, and not the old name? And at zero is the game untouched, and at one is everything gray, the player too?

Then point to the line that reads the screen.
